newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Sarajevo bank plans to open branch in Serb area.
newsitem.headline: Sarajevo bank plans to open branch in Serb area.

text.p: A Sarajevo bank said on Friday it had won permission to open an office in the country's Serb entity, making it the first company from the Moslem-Croat federation to operate in Serb-controlled territory since war ended 18 months ago.
The president of Promdei Bank, Ibrahim Dedic, said the national bank in the Bosnian Serb republic had granted a license for a branch office in the northwest town of Banja Luka.
"It has been approved," Dedic told Reuters.
"The negotiations have been going on for more than a month and now it's just a matter of paper work."
After receiving the license, Promdei bank could register in a Serb court and open the Banja Luka office within a couple of months, Dedic said.
The move, if confirmed, represented a rare exception by Serb nationalist authorities who tend to discourage commercial integration between their autonomous territory and the federation.
Serb authorities, who fought against Bosnian statehood during 3-1/2 years of war, have tried to prevent Moslems or Croats from visiting or moving back to their pre-war homes in the Banja Luka region.
A 1995 peace treaty divided Bosnia into autonomous territories governed under a loose union but the new central government has been bogged down in quarrels between rival political leaders.
Dedic said he planned to employ 12 ethnic Serbs in the Banja Luka office, which would cater to international aid organisations and local banks or companies transferring money from abroad.
Promdei bank, which has assets of 800 million dollars, was established in Croatia during the Yugoslav conflict and now has 27 branches in Bosnia, said Dedic, a Bosnian Moslem from the town of Bihac.
Dedic is no stranger to crossing former front lines to build up his banking network.
Promdei also has a branch in Croat-controlled western Mostar and the office has been targeted by three bombing attacks over the past year.
Dedic opened an office in the Serb enclave of Eastern Slavonia in Croatia two months ago, offering banking services in Yugoslav dinars, Croatian kuna and German marks.
Eastern Slavonia is under temporary United Nations administration and is due to be handed over to Croatian control later this year.
